To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
field dependence and dogmatism interact in a manner that affects peer choices of teaching competence.

(1) field independence and dogmatism interact to affect peer judgments of professional competence; (2) field dependent/highly-dogmatic persons were chosen least often; (3) field dependent/low-dogmatic persons and field independent/low-dog-matic persons were chosen equally often; and (4) the field independent/highly-dog-matic person was chosen more often than the field dependent/ low-dogmatic person.
field dependence and dogmatism interact in a manner that predicts a peer judgment criterion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and use of an objective criterion of professional competence and the theoretical relationships of this criterion to field independence and dogmatism.
the relationship between field independence and dogmatism and a judgment criterion of professional competency.
the relationship between two individual differences, field independence and dogmatism, on a criterion of peer judgment of professional competence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the peer judgment criterion of competence, as measured in this study, is related to the personality characteristics of field independence and dogmatism.
field independence and dogmatism are not directly related to professional competence, but are related to each other and are related to the peer judgment criterion of competence.
field dependence is a more important determinant of peer judgment than is dogmatism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

field independence and dogmatism are related, that the field independent/low dogmatic intern is more competent in the professional sense and more popular in the interpersonal sense, and that the field dependent/high dogmatic intern is least likely to be chosen as a peer by his colleagues.
the field dependent person is not necessarily less competent, but that the highly dogmatic person is less competent.
the field dependent person, who is more willing to accept and use information from others and to be influenced by them, is more likely to be chosen for competence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should not assume that a single personality trait will always predict a given criterion of performance.
we need to be more careful about how we define and measure professional competence.
we should be more careful when we use the terms “dogmatism” and “field independence” and should be more specific in how we define these concepts.
